In this chapter we'll develop our understanding of hypothesis testing by exploring some related concepts: effect size, inferential errors, and statistical power. These are nuanced ideas, and statistical power in particular can be difficult to get your head around both conceptually and computationally. But they are key to fully understanding the strengths and limitations of hypothesis testing, so we'll take our time with them here before moving on to other ideas and tests.

## NHST logic recap

First, let's recap the ideas we covered in the previous chapter as a way of refining our thinking and preparing for the new aspects we'll examine. We'll do so in a different way than before, not by looking at a single dataset or one boring old curve. Instead we'll use something more dynamic, more delightful, more fuzzy and yellow.

::::: {.callout-tip .interactive}
## NHST in action: a swarm of bees

:::: {.callout-footer}
::: {.tutorial-step data-major="swarm" data-major-title="Swarm" data-title="The swarm" data-action='{"variability":"high","sample-size":15,"hive-offset":0,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":false,"show-mean-line":false,"show-null-curve":false,"show-critical-regions":false,"show-histogram":false,"show-significance-tracker":false,"animate":false}'}
It's a swarm of bees! Well, a simulated swarm: little yellow circles following a flocking algorithm. Aren't they charming? Watch them buzz this way and that for a moment. They try not to bump into each other. And they always know where their hive is---the brown diamond in the middle. They venture away, but always return, bringing back little bits of pollen or whatever it is they're up to. Bees!
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="swarm" data-major-title="Swarm" data-title="Population and sample" data-action='{"variability":"high","sample-size":15,"hive-offset":0,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":false,"show-mean-line":false,"show-null-curve":false,"show-critical-regions":false,"show-histogram":false,"show-significance-tracker":false,"animate":false}'}
What does this have to do with null hypothesis significance testing, you may ask? Well, in this analogy, the hive at the center is the population mean, $\mu$. It is the real and unchanging center. The bees buzzing around it are a sample, constantly changing from one moment to the next as if we're drawing repeated samples from the population.^[Okay, listen, this is calibrated to offer an illustration of the sampling distribution, but it is not a demonstration of independent random sampling. The bees interact, and each bee's position is correlated from one frame to the next; a bee exploring to the left of the hive won't suddenly teleport off to the right. But the approximation is good enough for our purposes here. And come on, they're delightful little bees!] The sample at any particular instant gives a clue about those population characteristics. NHST offers one way of interpreting the clues.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="sampling" data-major-title="Sampling" data-title="One sample" data-action='{"variability":"high","sample-size":15,"hive-offset":0,"alpha":0.05,"playing":false,"pause-min-z":1,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":false,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":false,"show-critical-regions":false,"show-histogram":false,"show-significance-tracker":false,"animate":true}'}
We can freeze time. At this instant, the dashed line marks the average horizontal position of all the bees together: their sample mean, $M$. (We'll only care about horizontal position; the up-and-down motion is just for show.) It's close to the hive, but not exactly on it. That's sampling error, the discrepancy between the sample statistic and the population parameter.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="sampling" data-major-title="Sampling" data-title="The hidden hive" data-action='{"variability":"high","sample-size":15,"hive-offset":0,"alpha":0.05,"playing":false,"pause-min-z":1,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":false,"show-null-hive":false,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":false,"show-critical-regions":false,"show-histogram":false,"show-significance-tracker":false,"animate":true}'}
Now, what if we didn't know for sure where the hive was? I've hidden it, but it still exists and hasn't changed. We can only see the sample mean, $M$. If we were to use that as our estimate of the population mean, we know we wouldn't be exactly right, but we don't know the sample's exact error.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="null" data-major-title="Null test" data-title="The null hive" data-action='{"variability":"high","sample-size":15,"hive-offset":0,"alpha":0.05,"playing":false,"pause-min-z":1,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":false,"show-null-hive":true,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":false,"show-critical-regions":false,"show-histogram":false,"show-significance-tracker":false,"animate":true}'}
When we're really doing research, we usually don't know the true population mean. So under NHST, we specify a null hypothesis: a model in which the population mean has a particular value, $\mu_0$. I've replaced the hive with a dashed outline representing our null hypothesis about the hive's position. It so happens that we're exactly right; the null predicts that the hive is where it really is.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="null" data-major-title="Null test" data-title="Critical regions" data-action='{"variability":"high","sample-size":15,"hive-offset":0,"alpha":0.05,"playing":false,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":false,"show-null-hive":true,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":false,"show-significance-tracker":false,"animate":true}'}
So now we can describe the sampling distribution of the mean derived from that null hypothesis (its guess about the population center, as well as knowledge of the population variability, sample size, and normality, as we discussed in Chapter 7). We set alpha (here .05) and define the critical regions. When a sample mean is in those regions, we would reject the null hypothesis.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="null" data-major-title="Null test" data-title="Every instant" data-action='{"variability":"high","sample-size":15,"hive-offset":0,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":false,"show-null-hive":true,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":false,"show-significance-tracker":false,"animate":true}'}
Let's let the swarm get back to work. The mean jitters around the hive, occasionally straying quite far away but generally staying close to the hidden hive and its equivalent dashed null outline. Occasionally it is far enough away that we would reject the null for that sample at that moment. Remember, we know that the null here is true---it is right where the true population center is---so those rejections are mistakes, false alarms.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="null" data-major-title="Null test" data-title="Collect" data-action='{"variability":"high","sample-size":15,"hive-offset":0,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":false,"show-null-hive":true,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":true,"show-significance-tracker":true,"animate":true}'}
Let's start keeping track of the sample means, building a histogram of their positions over time. Watch the bees a while and see how the distribution forms. Or if you want to speed things along, click the fast-forward button to add a minute of simulated samples. We'll also track how much of that distribution falls into the critical regions of the null distribution, i.e. the proportion of samples that would lead us to reject the null. Over time, this proportion should be roughly five percent, because that's the definition of $\alpha = .05$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="alternative" data-major-title="False null" data-title="A different hive" data-action='{"variability":"high","sample-size":15,"hive-offset":38,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":true,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":false,"show-significance-tracker":false,"animate":true}'}
Now, what if the null is *wrong*? I'm going to show the hive again, and also move it over a bit. So now the null hive---the dashed outline---makes an incorrect prediction about where the true population center is. This changes our thought process a bit. Rather than risking falsely rejecting a correct null, we need to think about how likely it is we will *correctly* reject this wrong null. And what are the chances we will fail to reject it, making another kind of mistake?
:::
::::

:::::

The last step gives us an outline for the rest of this chapter. The distance between the null and the actual hive---the difference between the null and true population means---is an *effect size*. We'll first look at how to describe that difference relative to population variability, then examine the decisions and mistakes we can make, and finally arrive at the idea of *statistical power*, a method of quantifying how likely we are to detect a real effect.

## Effect Size

A "statistically significant" result, like the one we found for the sample of three Spider-People [in the previous chapter](#sec-spider-test), tells us that the observed test statistic is sufficiently improbable under the null model to meet our chosen criterion. It's a binary decision, reject or fail to reject the null; $p < \alpha$ or $p \ge \alpha$. It doesn't tell us how *big* the difference is. In everyday language, "significant" often means important, big, meaningful, but not in hypothesis testing. In this context, it only means we've met a statistical decision rule, nothing more or less.

The size of the difference *is* part of the $z$ equation from Chapter 8:

$$ z = \frac{M - \mu_0}{\sigma_M} $$

Here, $M$ is the sample mean, and $\mu_0$ is the mean specified by the null hypothesis, so the diffrerence between them is right there in the numerator. But that gets divided by the standard error, $\sigma_M$. You'll remember from the previous chapter that standard error is calculated by dividing the population standard deviation by a function of sample size, $\sigma_M = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$. For a given difference and population variability, increasing $n$ reduces the standard error and makes its $z$ more extreme. Even a tiny difference can therefore be statistically significant with a large enough sample. Conversely, a substantial difference can be nonsignificant with a small sample.

So the *significance* of the test is only part of the story. Measures of *effect size* describe the *magnitude* of a difference or relationship. For our one-sample test, we could report the raw difference, $M - \mu_0$, in the original units. The bigger the difference, the larger the effect. But it's often nice to have a standardized measure that allows us to compare effects across different studies and contexts.

### Cohen's $d$

One such standardized measure is Cohen's $d$. (Cohen didn't say so himself, but let's all agree that the $d$ stands for "difference.") For our $z$-test, where the population standard deviation is known, we calculate Cohen's $d$ as:

$$ d = \frac{M - \mu_0}{\sigma} $$ {#eq-cohens-d}

Notice how close that is to the sample $z$-score equation, $z = \frac{M - \mu_0}{\sigma_M}$. The numerator is exactly the same, but the denominator is the plain population standard deviation, $\sigma$, rather than the standard error. A value of $d = 0.5$ means the sample mean is half a population standard deviation above the null mean; $d = -0.5$ means it is half a standard deviation below. The sign tells us the direction, while the absolute value tells us the magnitude.

Unlike $z$, this calculation does not increase automatically with sample size: the same $M$, $\mu_0$, and $\sigma$ give the same $d$ regardless of $n$. So in this sense, the effect size is independent of sample size. (But $d$ calculated from a sample is still an estimate, and larger samples generally give more *precise* estimates of the population effect.)

### Effect size and statistical significance

Let's demonstrate the difference with a hypothetical study. Suppose we're educational psychologists trying to develop an intervention to boost students' SAT performance. And suppose we think we've hit upon an effective treatment: giving the test taker a banana just before taking the test. Maybe the potassium helps with cognitive function or something like that, who knows. For this example, let's say the relevant population without the treatment has a mean of $\mu = 500$ and a known standard deviation of $\sigma = 100$, making a $z$-test is appropriate. (And that we're sampling independently and the sampling distribution is normal.)

We choose a two-tailed test with $\alpha = .05$ before collecting data, making our critical values are $z \approx \pm 1.96$. After the banana treatment, we observe a sample mean of $M = 501$, one point above the null mean, $\mu_0 = 500$.

First, suppose the sample contains 50,000 students.

$$ z = \frac{M - \mu_0}{\sigma_M} = \frac{501 - 500}{100 / \sqrt{50{,}000}} \approx 2.24 $$

$$ d = \frac{M - \mu_0}{\sigma} = \frac{501 - 500}{100} = 0.01 $$

The result is statistically significant: $z$ exceeds 1.96. But the effect size is tiny, just one hundredth of a standard deviation.

Now suppose the same sample mean, $M = 501$, came from a sample of just 1,000 students.

$$ z = \frac{M - \mu_0}{\sigma_M} = \frac{501 - 500}{100 / \sqrt{1{,}000}} \approx 0.32 $$

$$ d = \frac{M - \mu_0}{\sigma} = \frac{501 - 500}{100} = 0.01 $$

In this case, the result is nonsignificant. The smaller sample produces a larger standard error and therefore a less extreme $z$. But both samples gave the same estimated effect: a difference of one point, or one hundredth of a standard deviation.

Assuming there really is a benefit to eating a banana before this test, one study was able to detect it and reject the null while the other failed to detect it (a kind of inferential error we'll describe more precisely a little later in the chapter). The sample size helped with statistical significance. But would supplying every student with a banana be a good use of resources? Significance alone can't answer that. A cheap intervention with a small benefit might be worthwhile; a costly one with the same benefit might not be. Effect size can help to inform that judgment.

### Interpreting Effect Size

This raises the question, what should we consider a meaningful effect size? Cohen outlined some rough rules of thumb: $d = .2$ could be considered a small effect, $d = .5$ medium, and $d = .8$ large. However, he cautioned *against* over-reliance on these guidelines. "The terms 'small,' 'medium,' and 'large' are relative, not only to each other, but to the area of behavioral science or even more particularly to the specific content and research method being employed in any given investigation," Cohen wrote. "In the face of this relativity, there is a certain risk inherent in offering conventional operational definitions for these terms" [@cohen1988power]. Cohen apparently regretted having taken that risk, because the rough guidelines came to be applied without much thought [@funder2019evaluating].

Taking Cohen's point about context-dependence to heart, @funder2019evaluating proposed a set of benchmarks specifc to the field of psychology. They arrived at these by drawing on published effect sizes across a range of psychological research.[^funder-ozer-conversion]

| $d$ | Description |
|-:|:---------------|
| 0.10 | Very small for the explanation of single events but potentially consequential in the longer run |
| 0.20 | Still small at the level of single events but potentially more ultimately consequential |
| 0.41 | Medium effect of some explanatory and practical use even in the short run |
| 0.63 | Large effect that is potentially powerful in both the short and the long run |
| 0.87 | A very large effect in the context of psychological research; likely to be a gross overestimate |

: Funder and Ozer's effect size benchmarks, converted from $r$ to approximate $d$ equivalents. {#tbl-funder-ozer}

[^funder-ozer-conversion]: They actually used the correlation coefficient, $r$, which we'll study in Chapter 17, as the measure of effect size. The table gives their benchmarks alongside approximate $d$ equivalents.These conversions use $d = 2r / \sqrt{1-r^2}$, the relationship for a comparison of two equally sized groups with equal within-group standard deviations [@cohen1988power, chap. 2].

Funder and Ozer stress that even very small effects can matter when they accumulate over time or affect many people. They also caution that unusually large estimates in psychological research should be scrutinized; not that very large effects cannot be real, but they are are uncommon within psychological research. Like Cohen's benchmarks, these guidelines need to be used with care and context.

### Effect sizes in context

What do differences of these sizes look like in practice? @simmons2014mturk reported the following examples. (These compare two groups rather than a sample with a fixed null mean, but $d$ still expresses the difference between means in standard deviation units.) @act-cohens-d visualizes these differences using smoothed curves based on the raw data.

| Groups compared | Outcome | Magnitude of $d$ |
|:--|:--|--:|
| Men / women | Height | 1.83 |
| Liberal / conservative | Importance of social equality | 0.69 |
| Like eggs / dislike eggs | Frequency of eating egg salad | 0.58 |
| Smoker / nonsmoker | Estimated risk of smoking-related death | 0.33 |
| Prefer science / prefer art | Number of planets named correctly | 0.05 |

::::: {#act-cohens-d .callout-tip .interactive}

Men and women's heights differed by $d = 1.83$ in Simmons' data: well beyond Cohen's large-effect benchmark of $0.8$. But notice that the distributions still overlap; there are some women are taller than some men, even though the averages are quite far apart.

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Social equality" data-action='{"example":"socialeq","show-slider":false}'}
Liberals and conservatives differed in the importance they placed on social equality by $d = 0.69$, measured on a 7-point scale. That's between Cohen's medium and large benchmarks, and just above the $d \approx 0.63$ equivalent of Funder and Ozer's large benchmark.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Egg salad" data-action='{"example":"eggsalad","show-slider":false}'}
People who liked and disliked eggs differed in how often they ate egg salad by $d = 0.58$. A difference that sounds obvious isn't necessarily enormous relative to individual variability.

Smokers and nonsmokers differed in their estimates of smoking-related mortality risk by $d = 0.33$. Notice that the curves don't have to be normal to calculate $d$; it is just a standardized difference between means.

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Naming planets" data-action='{"example":"planets","show-slider":false}'}
People who preferred science and those who preferred art differed in the number of planets they could name by just $d = 0.05$; in fact, in this case the difference was not statistically significant. The preference might be associated with other differences, but apparently not with this one.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Explore" data-action='{"d":0.05,"show-slider":true}'}
Try your own values, using these normal curves. Cohen's benchmarks are $d = 0.2$, $0.5$, and $0.8$; Funder and Ozer's very small and large benchmarks translate to about $0.10$ and $0.63$. Notice how the distance between means and overlap between distributions changes.
:::

## Errors in Hypothesis Testing

Null hypothesis significance testing is an *inferential* process, by which I mean we're using limited information from a sample to make a general conclusion (the inference) about a population. Hopefully we make the correct decision, rejecting null hypotheses when they are false and failing to reject them when they are true. But we don't have direct insight into what's really true in the world, we only have our limited and imperfect data and the inferences it supports to work with. We don't know which decision is correct. So it is possible to make the wrong decision.

Attaching some terms to these possibilities will help us think more precisely about them, and eventually quantify the likelihood of different outcomes.

There are only two decisions we can make: either we reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis. But there are two potential states of reality: either the null hypothesis is true or it is false. So there are four possible situations in total, shown in @tbl-inferenece-outcomes. Two of the four are correct decisions; our conclusion corresponds to reality. The other two are errors, where our conclusion does not match reality.

::: {#tbl-inferenece-outcomes}
<div class="table-responsive">
<table id="inf-tab" class="sfs-decision-table">
  <thead>
    <tr><th colspan=2></th><th colspan=2>Actual situation</th></tr>
    <tr><th colspan=2></th><th>$H_0$ true</th><th>$H_0$ false</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <th rowspan=2 class="sfs-decision-side">Researcher's<br>Decision</th>
      <th>Reject $H_0$</th>
      <td class="sfs-decision-error">Type 1 error<br>$\alpha$</td>
      <td class="sfs-decision-correct">Correct<br>$1-\beta$</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th>Fail to reject $H_0$</th>
      <td class="sfs-decision-correct">Correct</td>
      <td class="sfs-decision-error">Type 2 error<br>$\beta$</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
</div>

2x2 table
:::

Let's work through the possibilities, focusing on the two types of error.

### Type 1 Error (False Positive)

Starting with the top-left cell: the null hypothesis, $H_0$ is *true* in reality, but our test leads us to reject that null hypothesis. In other words, we might infer that there is an effect when there actually isn't. This is often called a **type one error**. A more useful description would be a *false positive*: thinking that there is an effect when actually there isn't.

The type one error, the false positive, is actually just another name for $\alpha$, the probability that we set as our cutoff criterion for unlikely results. An $\alpha$ of .05, for example, is an acknowledgement that *if the null hypothesis is correct*, we would see sample means like this five percent of the time. If we ran our experiment 100 times we could expect to reject our null hypothesis five out of those 100 times, if the null is correct.

Maybe this sounds bad. Why tolerate a 5% chance of a false positive? Well, given the inferential nature of hypothesis testing, we have to tolerate *some* risk. Too little tolerance and we would never be able to produce satisfying evidence of real effects; too much tolerance and we would be prone to false positives. Using a alpha of .05 became the convention within psychology and much of the social sciences. Like I mentioned in the previous chapter, it puts the threshold at close to 2 standard deviations of a difference, which is a reasonable balance between sensitivity and specificity. But it's not a magic number. There are good arguments that five percent is too high and that we should more often use a lower $\alpha$ value of 1 percent or even .1 percent in order to reduce the chances of making a type one error. That's an ongoing debate and one you might hear more about in more advanced research methods or stats classes.

In the bottom-left cell, we are still saying that in reality the null is true, there is no real effect. But in this case, we fail to reject the null: our data leads us to infer that there is no effect. In that case, we have made the correct decision. The probability of making the correct decision when the null is true is $1 - \alpha$. Each column of the table, $H_0$ true and $H_0$ false, represents one possible state of reality; given a true null, either we reject it or not. Those two options cover all the bases and so their two probabilities must sum to 1. So if the probability of making a type one error is $\alpha$, then the probability of making the correct decision when the null is true is $1 - \alpha$.

### Type 2 Error (False Negative)

Moving over to the right-hand column of @tbl-inferenece-outcomes, here we are saying that in reality $H_0$ is *false*. Still, we either reject of fail to reject the null. So now the possibilites are correctly rejecting or mistakenly failing to reject that false null. This is the opposite kind of mistake from the type one error. The null hypothesis is false, but our data failed to show persuasive enough evidence of an effect. This is called a **type two error**. A more useful description would be a *false negative*: thinking that there is no effect when actually there is.

The probability of making a type two error is referred to as $\beta$. Given the names, you might be tempted to think that $\beta$ is just the flip side of $\alpha$, but it's not. Each column of the table represents a different possible state of reality; they are independent of one another, and they each have their own probabilities. I said that the probabilities of two cells belonging to the left-hand column sum to 1 (they were $\alpha$ and $1 - \alpha$). The same is true for the right-hand column: the probabilities of the two cells in that column must also sum to 1. So if the probability of making a type two error is $\beta$, then the probability of making the correct decision when the null is false is $1 - \beta$. That quantity has a name of its own: it is called the *statistical power* of the test.

## Statistical Power

The power of a test is defined as the probability that the test will reject the null hypothesis *if the treatment really does have an effect*. We're not saying that we know for sure that the null is false; we're just supposing that it is, and asking how likely it is that we will correctly reject it. It's not a quantity that we arbitrarily set, like $\alpha$; it is a property of the test itself, given the sample size, variability, and effect size. If we know (or can make assumptions about) those quantities, we can calculate the power of a test precisely.

To illustrate, let's check in with our bees again.

::::: {#act-bees-2 .callout-tip .interactive}
## Watch power in action: the swarm returns

{{< interactive-figure beeSwarmPower makeBeeSwarm options='{"seed":"bee-swarm-power-v121","variability":"high","n":15,"hiveOffset":0,"playing":false,"displayScale":1.6,"densityMaximum":0.05,"showEffectSize":false,"showStandardError":false,"collectWhenVisible":true,"tutorialFastForward":true}' fallback="Animated bee swarm illustrating statistical power: when the hive moves away from the null position, the proportion of sample means that land in the critical regions is the power of the test, and it rises with sample size and effect size and falls with variability." >}}

:::: {.callout-footer}
::: {.tutorial-step data-major="null" data-major-title="True null" data-title="False alarms" data-action='{"variability":"high","sample-size":15,"hive-offset":0,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"advance":0,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":true,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":true,"show-significance-tracker":true,"animate":true}'}
When we first introduced the bees, they were buzzing around a hive that was exactly where the null hypothesis predicted it to be. The sample means were piling up around the null, and occasionally one would land in a critical region, leading us to reject the null. But since the null was true, those rejections were mistakes: false positives, type I errors. Over time, the proportion of sample means that landed in the critical regions should settle near $\alpha = .05$, as expected.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="power" data-major-title="False null" data-title="Move the hive" data-action='{"variability":"high","sample-size":15,"hive-offset":38,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"advance":0,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":true,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":false,"show-significance-tracker":false,"animate":true}'}
Then we moved the hive. This illustrates another possible reality, in which the null hypothesis is false. The two possible outcomes are that we will either fail to reject the null (a Type 2 error, denoted $\beta$), or that we will correctly reject the null ($1 - \beta$).
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="power" data-major-title="Null false" data-title="Critical regions" data-action='{"variability":"high","sample-size":15,"hive-offset":38,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"advance":0,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":true,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":false,"show-significance-tracker":false,"animate":true}'}
How can we figure out what those proportions are? Well, we already defined the critical regions for the null hypothesis. They don't change just because the null is false. They still tell us which sample means would lead us to reject that null, and which would not.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="power" data-major-title="Null false" data-title="Where the means land" data-action='{"variability":"high","sample-size":15,"hive-offset":38,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"advance":0,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":true,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":true,"show-significance-tracker":false,"animate":true}'}
So now we'll just collect sample means for a while and see where they pile up. The swarm is still jittering around the true hive, and the sample means are piling up in its vicinity. Some of those sample means will land in the critical regions of the null distribution, and some will not. The ones that land in the critical regions are correct rejections of the null hypothesis. The ones that land between the critical boundaries are Type 2 errors. The proprtion of those false negatives gives us $\beta$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="power" data-major-title="Null false" data-title="Power" data-action='{"variability":"high","sample-size":15,"hive-offset":38,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"advance":0,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":true,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":true,"show-significance-tracker":true,"animate":true}'}
So to quantify the statical power of our bees here, all we have to do is turn back on the tracker and check the "proportion sigfnicant" value. That's the proportion of the sample means in the critical regions, which would cause us to reject the null hypothesis and declare a significant result. $\beta$, the proportion of sample means that land *between* the critical regions, is the probability of a Type 2 error.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="factors" data-major-title="Factors" data-title="More bees" data-action='{"variability":"high","sample-size":50,"hive-offset":38,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"advance":0,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":true,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":true,"show-significance-tracker":true,"animate":true}'}
We'll walk through calculating power when we don't have a swarm of bees to watch shortly, but let's think about what factors might affect a test's power. What if the hive's true position was closer to the null's prediction, or farther away? What if we increased the number of bees here? Or reduced how far they can wander from the hive? Right now, power is around .7. Let's see how that value changes.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="factors" data-major-title="Factors" data-title="Calmer swarm" data-action='{"variability":"medium","sample-size":15,"hive-offset":19,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"advance":0,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":true,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":true,"show-significance-tracker":true,"animate":true}'}
First we'll move the hive closer to the null, reducing effect size. If you let the bees buzz around a while (or click the fast-forward button), you'll see that their yellow sampling distribution moves over with the hive, and more of it lands in the nonsignificant region of the null curve. Correspondingly, power---the proportion significant---is reduced.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="factors" data-major-title="Factors" data-title="Smaller effect" data-action='{"variability":"high","sample-size":15,"hive-offset":19,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"advance":0,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":true,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":true,"show-significance-tracker":true,"animate":true}'}
Now what if we reduce the population variability: the bees stick closer to their hive. Their yellow distribution becomes narrower, centered on their hive. And the null distribution, responding to the reduced population standard deviation in its standard error, shrinks. This brings the critical regions in closer to the null hive, with the result that more of the sample means land in the critical regions. Power increases.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="factors" data-major-title="Factors" data-title="Stricter alpha" data-action='{"variability":"high","sample-size":15,"hive-offset":38,"alpha":0.01,"playing":true,"advance":0,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":true,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":true,"show-significance-tracker":true,"animate":true}'}
Let's add more bees, increasing the sample size. The standard error shrinks again, this time responding to the larger $n$ in its denominator. The sample means pile up more tightly around the true hive. More of them land in the critical regions, and power increases again.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="bridge" data-major-title="Our example" data-title="Back to our example" data-action='{"variability":"high","sample-size":15,"hive-offset":38,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"advance":0,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":true,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":true,"show-significance-tracker":true,"animate":true}'}
We'll explore these factors more systematically in the next section, but for now let's reset to our original 15 bees producing a test with a power of around .70. That means that if we were to repeat this experiment many times, we would correctly reject the null hypothesis about 70% of the time. The bees here provide an empirical demonstration of that figure, but moving on we'll show how to calculate it based on the test parameters.
:::
::::

:::::


### Calculating Power

The bees are cute and all, but how do we actually calculate statistical power in practice? For that, we'll need some step-by-step instructions. I'll also show you how it looks visualized with some boring old curves, because unfortunately we can't always do statistics with bees.

The key idea is that we need to think about two distributions: the null hypothesis distribution and the alternative hypothesis distribution. The null hypothesis distribution represents what we would expect to see if the null hypothesis were true, while the alternative hypothesis distribution represents what we would expect to see if the alternative hypothesis were true. This requires having some idea of what the alternative hypothesis is, which is usually based on prior research or theory. Applying this in the context of the $z$-test we used in the previous chapter means we also need to know the population standard deviation. (We can apply statistical power in the context of other tests as well.)

Here are the steps we need to follow to calculate statistical power:

1. Find the null distribution's critical values, given $\alpha$
2. Find the corresponding null distribution sample means for those critical values
3. Find the corresponding $z$ scores for those sample means under the alternative hypothesis distribution
4. Find the area of the alternative distribution that falls between those $z$ scores, which is $\beta$, the probability of a type two error
5. Subtract $\beta$ from 1 to get the statistical power of the test

Let's work through the steps with some real numbers, illustrating what happens at each step along the way. 

$\mu_0 = 50$; $\sigma = 38.73$; $n = 15$; $\sigma_M = 10$; $\mu_1 = 74$.

Step 1. We first focus our attention on the null distribution. We need to determine the critical $z$ scores that define its critical regions, which contain the results that will cause us to reject the null hypothesis. Assuming we're dealing with a normal sampling distribution, we we can use the unit normal table to find those scores. So let's say our $\alpha$ is .05. We'd find critical $z$ scores of $\pm 1.96$. Notice, so far this is just the regular decision-criterion step of the NHST procedure.

{{< interactive-figure powerCriticalZTable makeCriticalValueTable options='{"distribution":"normal","layout":"areas","title":"Unit normal table (excerpt)","z":{"from":1.92,"to":2.0,"step":0.01},"zDigits":2,"areas":["left","right","mean-to-z"],"selected":{"z":1.96,"area":"right"},"maxWidth":"32rem"}' fallback="Excerpt of the unit normal table for z from 1.92 to 2.00, with the area to the right of z = 1.96, .0250, highlighted." >}}

Step 2 is to determine what original sample means those critical $z$ scores correspond to. To do that, we use the rearranged form of the $z$ equation we first encountered in Chapter 5. Here, since we're using the null distributions characteristics, that becomes:

$$ M = \mu_0 + z \cdot \sigma_M $$

We obtained two z-scores in step one, corresponding to the two-tailed critical regions. (Statistical power can work with a one-tailed test as well; we would only have a single critical $z$-score in that case.) So we can plug those into the equation, with the $\mu_0$ and the standard error to get the corresponding sample means.

$$ M_{lower} = 50 + (-1.96) \cdot 10 = 30.40 $$

$$ M_{upper} = 50 + (1.96) \cdot 10 = 69.60 $$

Step 3. Now we turn our attention to the alternative hypothesis distribution. We need to know its center. Here we said we expect a difference of $+24$ units, which centers the distribution on $\mu_1 = 74$, compared to $\mu_0 = 50$. The standard error is the same as before, because the sample size and population standard deviation are the same.

Now we need to work out what $z$ scores correspond to the sample means we just worked out, but for this distribution.

{{< include quizzes/09-power-alternative-means.qmd >}}

Step 4. Now we can find the proportion of the alternative distribution that falls between those $z$ scores. Using the unit normal table, we subtract the area to the left of the lower boundary from the area to the left of the upper boundary. The area to the left of $z = -0.44$ is the same as the area to the right of $z = 0.44$, which the table gives as .3300, and the area to the left of $z = -4.36$ is so far out in the tail that it rounds to .0000: $.3300 - .0000 = .3300$. This gives us the area of the region shaded gray here. This is the proportion of the alternative distribution that will cause us to fail to reject the null hypothesis, making a type two, false negative error. Remember, we refer to this quantity as $\beta$.

{{< interactive-figure powerBetaZTable makeCriticalValueTable options='{"distribution":"normal","layout":"areas","title":"Unit normal table (excerpt)","z":{"from":0.4,"to":0.48,"step":0.01},"zDigits":2,"areas":["left","right","mean-to-z"],"selected":{"z":0.44,"area":"right"},"maxWidth":"32rem"}' fallback="Excerpt of the unit normal table for z from 0.40 to 0.48, with the area to the right of z = 0.44, .3300, highlighted." >}}

Step 5. Finally we can work out the statistical power of the test---the chances of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis---by working out the area of the rest of the distribution. This is just $1 - \beta$, because it has to add up to 1. So for this example, we had a 33.0% chance of making a type two error, leaving us with a 67.0% chance of making the correct decision to reject the null hypothesis. So the power of the test is .670.

Given our stated sample size here, and population standard deviations and means, if we could run this experiment 100 times, we would successfully reject our null hypothesis 67.0% of the time.

::::: {#act-calculating-power .callout-tip .interactive .with-controls}
## Explore statistical power

{{< interactive-figure statisticalPower makeStatisticalPowerDiagram options='{"mu":50,"sigma":38.73,"n":15,"d":0.62,"alpha":0.05,"showAlt":false,"shadeBeta":false,"shadePower":false,"axisZNull":true,"axisRaw":false}' fallback="Explore statistical power. Use the accompanying steps for an explanation." >}}

:::: {.callout-footer}
::: {.tutorial-step data-title="The null" data-action='{"mu":50,"sigma":38.73,"n":15,"effect-size":0.62,"alpha":0.05,"two-tailed":true,"shade-beta":false,"shade-power":false,"dim-h0":false,"show-H1":false,"raw-scores":false,"h0-z":true,"h1-z":false}'}
Start with a null population mean of 50, a population SD of 38.73, and samples of 15. The standard error is $38.73 / \sqrt{15} \approx 10$. This curve shows sample means under the null, labeled in $z$ units. For a two-tailed test with $\alpha = .05$, the critical $z$ values are about $\pm 1.96$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Critical means" data-action='{"mu":50,"sigma":38.73,"n":15,"effect-size":0.62,"alpha":0.05,"two-tailed":true,"shade-beta":false,"shade-power":false,"dim-h0":false,"show-H1":false,"raw-scores":true,"h0-z":true,"h1-z":false}'}
On the raw-score ruler, those same boundaries are $50 - 1.96(10) = 30.40$ and $50 + 1.96(10) = 69.60$. Sample means outside these boundaries lead us to reject the null. Keep those raw-score boundaries in mind: we will use the same decision rule when we consider a population where the null is false.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="A specified alternative" data-action='{"mu":50,"sigma":38.73,"n":15,"effect-size":0.62,"alpha":0.05,"two-tailed":true,"shade-beta":false,"shade-power":false,"dim-h0":true,"show-H1":true,"raw-scores":true,"h0-z":false,"h1-z":false}'}
Suppose the true population mean is 74 instead. That's a difference of 24 units, or $d \approx 0.62$, because the population SD is 38.73. Samples of 15 from this alternative population have a sampling distribution centered on 74, still with a standard error of 10. The violet areas show the sample means that would cross the null's rejection boundaries.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="The alternative ruler" data-action='{"mu":50,"sigma":38.73,"n":15,"effect-size":0.62,"alpha":0.05,"two-tailed":true,"shade-beta":true,"shade-power":false,"dim-h0":true,"show-H1":true,"raw-scores":true,"h0-z":false,"h1-z":true}'}
Now read the boundaries relative to the alternative mean. The lower one is $(30.40 - 74) / 10 = -4.36$ standard errors below it; the upper one is $(69.60 - 74) / 10 = -0.44$. The boundaries are still at the same raw scores. We've changed the ruler we use to describe them.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Misses and detections" data-action='{"mu":50,"sigma":38.73,"n":15,"effect-size":0.62,"alpha":0.05,"two-tailed":true,"shade-beta":true,"shade-power":true,"dim-h0":true,"show-H1":true,"raw-scores":true,"h0-z":false,"h1-z":true}'}
The gray area under the alternative curve lies between the critical boundaries. These samples fail to reject a false null: $\beta \approx .330$. The violet area outside the boundaries is power: $1 - \beta \approx .670$. So this design detects this particular effect about 67 percent of the time over repeated studies. Both rejection tails count, though the far-left contribution here is tiny.
:::

::::
:::::

### Factors Affecting Power

Having worked through calculating power with a particular set of parameters, it's worth spending some time thinking about how changing different quantities will affect power. Increasing effect size, the distance between the means, increases power because the distributions will be farther apart and overlap less. Increasing sample size also increases power because it reduces the standard error, again meaning that the distributions will overlap less. Reducing our $\alpha$ value lowers power because it makes for a more stringent test. The critical regions of the null distribution will be smaller and so less of the alternative distribution will cause us to reject the null. And the directionality of our hypothesis affects power as well. Using a one-tailed test increases power since it gives a larger critical region in one tail that we're interested in.

If you really understand how and why each of these factors affects power, you'll have a good grasp of the concept.

### Practical Applications of Power

Since this is all quite abstract, you may be wondering the usefulness of knowing about statistical power. And honestly, it has long been overlooked within psychology. Until recently, it was quite rare for a published research paper to even mention statistical power. But it's now generally accepted that power should be a central feature of research design.

Researchers could calculate the power of a study before beginning their research or after a study has been conducted, using their knowledge or their assumptions about effect size, sample size, and $\alpha$. But a more practically useful use of power is to specify the power you want in advance and adjust your required sample size in order to achieve that level of power. This requires knowing or estimating your expected effect size. And then you can say, for example, that you want a power of .8 or an 80 percent chance of detecting a real effect of that size. And then you can calculate how many participants you need in order to achieve that level of power.

### Power in Context: Real-World Examples

Let's return to the differences we pictured in @act-cohens-d. @simmons2014mturk also reported the sample sizes needed to detect them with 80 percent power:

| Outcome | Magnitude of $d$ | $n$ per group for 80% power |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Height | 1.83 | 6 |
| Importance of social equality | 0.69 | 33 |
| Frequency of eating egg salad | 0.58 | 47 |
| Estimated risk of smoking-related death | 0.33 | 149 |
| Number of planets named correctly | 0.05 | 6,176 |

These are the authors' reported sample sizes for comparisons of two groups; $n$ is **per group**. They are not calculations for the one-sample $z$ test we used above.

So, for example, given the real average difference between men and women's heights, you'd need around twelve people, six men and six women, to have sufficient statistical power to detect it. The difference between men and women's heights is very large, with a Cohen's $d$ of around 1.83. So you don't need many participants to reliably detect it.

Usually, though, psychologists are interested in more subtle differences. You might think the difference between liberals and conservatives in terms of how important they say social equality is would be pretty robust. But given its effect size of around .7, you already need many more participants, around 33 each of liberals and conservatives, or almost 70 participants total, in order to have a power of .8 to detect the difference.

This paper also included some questions that sound kind of funny, like comparing people who say they do or do not like eggs in terms of how often they eat egg salad. You'd think this would be a pretty easy effect to detect, but you'd need close to 100 participants to reliably detect it.

A lot of psychology has to do with attitudes and behaviors that we aren't entirely aware of, like motivated cognition. It seems pretty plausible that smokers would underestimate the likelihood of a smoker dying from a smoking-related illness as compared to nonsmokers. And they do. But it's a small enough effect that you'd need almost 300 people in your study to detect it with 80 percent power.

And lastly, people who say they prefer science over art can name more of the planets than people who say they prefer art. Again, it's plausible that this would be the case, but it's a very small difference. If you didn't know the size of the difference in advance, you'd need a study with more than 12,000 people to have 80 percent power to detect the difference.

So this is all worth bearing in mind when you read papers for other classes. Think about the sample sizes they had, the subtlety of the effects that they're looking for, and whether they really had sufficient power to detect those effects.

I'll end with a quote here by <!-- [Possible typo: "by its statistical power" in original; likely meant "about statistical power"] --> Stuart Ritchie from *Science Fictions*, which is a great recent book about the scientific method and the uses and misuses of statistics. The author noted that running a study with low statistical power is like setting out to look for distant galaxies with a pair of binoculars. Even if what you're looking for is definitely out there, you have essentially no chance of seeing it. And I would add, anything you do see may not be quite what you think it is.
